hints: Look closely at what statements 1, 2 and 3 are all saying about immunity and antigens, and ask yourself which diseases would be hard to vaccinate against for a long time.
Remember that a successful eradication vaccine needs stable antigens for long-lasting memory, and that vaccines can protect against bacteria as well as viruses, so check statement 4 carefully.
walkthrough:
**Test statement 4 first because it is the easiest to check**

Statement 4 says vaccines only work against viruses. That is not true.

We use vaccines against bacteria too, for example cholera, tuberculosis, diphtheria and tetanus. So any option containing 4 must be wrong.

**Think about what makes smallpox easy to eradicate**

Statement 3 says smallpox antigens remain stable. That is true and very important.

Stable antigens mean the vaccine always recognises the virus, so memory B and T cells give strong, long-lasting immunity in almost everyone.

**Think about what makes cholera and malaria hard to eradicate**

Statement 1 is true. Cholera vaccines give only short-term immunity, so protection fades and transmission continues.

Statement 2 is also true. Plasmodium has a complex life cycle in mosquito and human, and it changes its surface antigens. This confuses the immune system and makes an effective long-lasting vaccine very difficult.

So 1, 2 and 3 are all correct, which is option A.

options.A: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 3 are all true and together explain stable, long-term vaccine success for smallpox but short-term or difficult immunity for cholera and malaria.
options.B: Incorrect. Although 1 and 2 are true, 4 is false because vaccines also work against many bacteria, not only viruses.
options.C: Incorrect. Although 1 and 3 are true, 4 is false for the same reason, vaccines protect against bacterial diseases too.
options.D: Incorrect. Although 2 and 3 are true, 4 is false, so this combination cannot be correct.
